newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: Press under pressure in riot-torn Guiana.
newsitem.headline: Press under pressure in riot-torn Guiana.

text.p: Journalists have come under pressure and are increasingly victims of violence while covering riots that have swept French Guiana in the last six months, a local reporters' group said on Friday.

"It's becoming more and more difficult and we are seeing a decline in the working conditions of journalists," Alexandre Rozga, president of the French Guiana Press Club, told local state-owned television.

While no deaths have been reported among journalists in France's South American territory, Rozga said reporters have been attacked on numerous occasions covering clashes between police and demonstrators.
Newspaper editors have received death threats at their homes. Camera crews have been victims of ethnic slurs and government officials have imposed censorship on certain local media.

The latest violence last month was triggered by the arrest and detention of 10 people, including four leading members of French Guiana's independence movement, for allegedly setting fire to the residence of French Guiana's state prosecutor during a previous wave of rioting in November.

Paramilitary riot police flown in from mainland France clashed with hooded and armed demonstrators in the capital Cayenne for three nights. Police fired teargas to disperse crowds. Rioters fired hunting rifles and threw Molotov cocktail firebombs, witnesses said.
Officials said 11 police have been injured during the three nights, 10 by gunfire. One civilian bystander lost an eye when a teargas grenade fired by police exploded in his face.
The riots have shattered French Guiana's tranquil facade and laid bare economic, political and social woes.
French Guiana is the only non-independent territory on the mainland of the Western Hemisphere.
It lags behind mainland France in housing, education and health. Its economy is heavily dependent on subsidies from France and 23 percent of the population of 150,000 is unemployed.

The Paris-based press watchdog group Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said that world-wide, the reporters' trade remained a dangerous one despite a significant drop in the number of journalists killed in 1996.

In a report released to mark international press freedom day on May 3, RSF said: " A total of 28 (journalists) paid with their lives for their courage in exposing unacceptable behaviour by those in power." The report listed 20 other journalists whose deaths were under investigation and 64 more who were missing on Jan. 1, 1997.
The situation for Latin America was varied, with Cuba, Mexico, Colombia and Guatemala singled out for criticism.
